front.title: Fast failure detection in VRRP with Point-to-Point BFD

abstract.t: This document describes how Point-to-Point Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can be used to support sub-second detection of an Active Router failure in the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP). This document updates RFC 9568.

section.name: Introduction
section.t:
The Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) provides redundant Virtual gateways in the Local Area Network (LAN), which is typically the first point of failure for end-hosts sending traffic out of the LAN. Fast failure detection of VRRP Active is critical in supporting high availability of services and improved Quality of Experience to users.
In VRRP specification, Backup Routers depend on VRRP packets generated at a regular interval by the Active Router, to detect the health of the VRRP Active. Faster failure detection can be achieved within VRRP protocol by reducing the Advertisement and Active Down Interval. However, sub-second Advert timers, can put extra load on CPU and the network bandwidth which may not be desirable.

Since the VRRP protocol depends on the availability of Layer 3 IPv4 or IPv6 connectivity between redundant peers, the VRRP protocol can interact with the Layer 3 variant of BFD as described in to achieve a much faster failure detection of the VRRP Active on the LAN. BFD, as specified by the can provide a much faster failure detection in the range of 150ms, if implemented in the part of a Network device which scales better than VRRP when sub-second Advert timers are used.

Terminology of this draft has been updated conform to inclusive language guidelines for VRRP Inclusive Terminologies . The IETF has designated National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) "Guidance for NIST Staff on Using Inclusive Language in Documentary Standards" for its inclusive language guidelines.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the terminology defined in Section 1.7 of . The following terms are used by this specification:

dl.dd: The VRRP Router currently responsible for forwarding packets sent to the IPvX addresses associated with the Virtual Router.
A VRRP Router available to assume forwarding responsibility if the current Active Router fails.
A VRRP packet with Type 2, sent by a Backup Router to advertise its presence and priority.
Per-Virtual-Router state learned from the source addresses of Advertisements and Backup Advertisements and used to identify VRRP peers.
The highest-priority Backup Router, with ties resolved using the primary IPvX address as specified in this document.
The point-to-point BFD session between the current Active Router and the Critical Backup.
The association of a Virtual Router instance with its current Critical Path BFD Session.

An Up-to-Down transition of the Critical Path BFD Session referenced by the current Critical BFD Binding. At a Backup Router, such a transition is eligible only while the local router is the currently selected Critical Backup for that Virtual Router.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Applicability of Point-to-Point BFD
section.t: BFD for IPv4 or IPv6 (Single Hop) requires that in order for a BFD session to be formed both peers participating in a BFD session need to know its peer IPv4 or IPv6 address. This poses a unique problem with the definition of the VRRP protocol, that makes the use of BFD for IPv4 or IPv6 more challenging. In VRRP it is only the Active Router that sends Advert packets. This means that an Active Router is not aware of any Backup Routers, and Backup Routers are only aware of the Active Router. This also means that a Backup Router is not aware of any other Backup Routers in the Network.

Since BFD for IPv4 or IPv6 requires that a session be formed by both peers using a full destination and source address, there needs to be some external means to provide this information to BFD on behalf of VRRP. Once the peer information is available, the current Active Router and the selected Critical Backup form the Critical Path BFD Session for the Virtual Router. This mechanism does not require a full mesh of BFD sessions among the VRRP Routers. An Eligible BFD Failure is interpreted as an Active Down event only by the currently selected Critical Backup. Other Backup Routers remain in the Backup state and continue to use the Active_Down_Timer, including the Skew_Time procedures specified by .
NOTE: At all times, the normal fail-over mechanism defined in the VRRP will be unaffected, and the BFD fail-over mechanism will always resort to normal VRRP fail-over.

This document defines the mechanism used by VRRP to build a Peer Table, select the Critical Backup, and form the Critical Path BFD Session. An Eligible BFD Failure signals an Active Down event only at the current Critical Backup. This requires an extension to the VRRP protocol.
This can be achieved by defining a new type in the VRRP Advert packet, and allowing VRRP peers to build a peer table in any of the operational state, Active or Backup.

section.name: Extension to VRRP protocol
section.t: In this mode of operation, VRRP Routers learn adjacent VRRP Routers. All Backup Routers periodically send BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT packets so that the participating routers can build the Peer Table and select the Critical Backup. The Active Router continues to send ADVERTISEMENT packets as defined by . Only the current Active Router and the selected Critical Backup form the Critical Path BFD Session.

Additionally, Advert packets sent from Backup Peers must not use the Virtual router MAC address as the source address. Instead it must use the Interface MAC address as the source address from which the packet is sent from. This is because the source MAC override feature is used by the Active to send Advert packets from the Virtual Router MAC address, which is used to keep the bridging cache on LAN switches and bridging devices refreshed with the destination port for the Virtual Router MAC.

section.name: VRRP Peer Table
section.t: VRRP peers form the Peer Table by learning the source address of the enclosing IPv4 or IPv6 packet carrying an ADVERTISEMENT or BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT. For IPv4, this is the sender's primary IPv4 address; for IPv6, this is the sender's interface link-local address, as specified by . This learned source address, and not an address in the protected IPvX address list, identifies the peer and the endpoint of the Critical Path BFD Session.
A peer entry should be removed from the peer table if Advert is not received from a peer for a period of (3 * the Advert interval).

section.name: VRRP BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT Packet Type
section.t: The following figure shows the VRRP packet as defined in VRRP RFC.

The type field specifies the type of this VRRP packet. The type field can have two values. Type 1 (ADVERTISEMENT) is used by the VRRP Active Router. Type 2 (BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT) is used by the VRRP Backup Router. This is to distinguish the packets sent by the VRRP Backup Router. VRRP Backup fills Backup_Advertisement_Interval in the Max Advert Int of BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT packet. The remaining fields are encoded as specified for an ADVERTISEMENT by .
A packet with unknown type MUST be discarded.

A BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT MUST carry the Count IPvX Addr and IPvX Address(es) fields for the same Virtual Router in the same manner as an ADVERTISEMENT. The minimum Count IPvX Addr is one; a packet with a count of zero MUST be ignored. Receivers MUST apply the applicable address-list validation from Section 7.1 of . The listed addresses identify the IPvX addresses protected by the Virtual Router; they are not BFD endpoints. The BFD endpoint is learned from the source address of the enclosing IPv4 or IPv6 packet.

section.name: Sample configuration
section.t: The following figure shows a simple network with three VRRP routers implementing one virtual router.
section.artwork: +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Rtr1 | | Rtr2 | | Rtr3 | |(AR VRID=1)| |(BR VRID=1)| |(BR VRID=1)| | (PR=200) | | (PR=150) | | (PR=100) | | VRIPVX= A | | VRIPVX= A | | VRIPVX= A | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ B C D | | | | | | | | | ---------+--------+--------+---------+--------+--------- Legend: ---+---+---+-- = Ethernet, Token Ring, or FDDI AR = Active Router BR = Backup Router PR = VRRP Router priority VRID = Virtual Router Identifier VRIPVX= IPv4 or IPv6 address protected by the VRRP Router B,C,D = Interface IPv4 or IPv6 address of the Virtual Router
section.t: In the above configuration there are three routers on the LAN protecting an IPv4 or IPv6 address associated to a Virtual Router Identifier 1. Rtr1 is the Active Router since it has the highest priority compared to Rtr2 and Rtr3. Now if peer learning extension is enabled on all the peers. Rtr1 will send the Advert packet with type field set to 1. While Rtr2 and Rtr3 will send the Advert packet with type field set to 2. In the above configuration the peer table built at each router is shown below:
Rtr1 Peer table
Rtr2 Peer table
Rtr3 Peer table

Once the Peer Tables are formed, each router independently selects Rtr2 as the Critical Backup. Rtr1 and Rtr2 form the Critical Path BFD Session. Rtr3 does not act on that session and continues to use the normal VRRP Active_Down_Timer.

section.name: Critical BFD session
section.t: Each router selects the Critical Backup from the Backup Routers for the Virtual Router, including the local router when it is in the Backup state. The Backup Router with the highest VRRP Priority is selected. If two or more Backup Routers have equal Priority, the one with the highest primary IPvX source address is selected using the address ordering specified by . The Critical BFD Session is formed only between the current Active Router and this selected Critical Backup.

In the above example, the Critical BFD Session is formed between Rtr1 and Rtr2. If that session transitions from Up to Down while Rtr2 remains the selected Critical Backup, Rtr2 treats the transition as an Active Down event, immediately assumes the Active role for VRID 1, and sends a Type 1 ADVERTISEMENT. Rtr3 does not change state in response to that BFD transition. It remains in Backup state and continues to use the Active_Down_Timer and Skew_Time procedures in .

A Backup Router MUST map an Up-to-Down transition of the Critical BFD Session to an Active Down event only when the local router is the currently selected Critical Backup for that Virtual Router. A Backup Router that is not the Critical Backup MUST NOT change its VRRP state as a result of that BFD session-state transition.

section.name: Parameters Per Virtual Router
section.t: Following parameters are added to the VRRP protocol to support this mode of operation.
section.artwork:
Backup_Advertisement_Interval Time interval between BACKUP ADVERTISEMENTS (centiseconds). Default is 100 centiseconds (1 second).
Backup_Adver_Interval Advertisement interval contained in BACKUP ADVERTISEMENTS received from the Backup (centiseconds). This value is saved by virtual routers used, to compute Backup_Down_Interval.
Backup_Down_Interval Time interval for VRRP instance to declare Backup down (centiseconds). Calculated as (3 * Backup_Adver_Interval) for each VRRP Backup.
Critical_Backup The highest-ranked Backup selected using the procedure described in the Critical BFD session section of this document.
Critical_BFD_Session The Critical BFD Session is the session between the VRRP Active and Critical_Backup.
Critical_BFD_Binding Associates this Virtual Router instance with its current Critical_BFD_Session.

section.name: Timers
section.t: Following timers are added to the VRRP protocol to support this mode of operation.
section.artwork:
Backup_Down_Timer Timer that fires when BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT has not been heard from a backup peer for Backup_Down_Interval.
Backup_Adver_Timer Timer that fires to trigger sending of BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT based on Backup_Advertisement_Interval.

section.name: Scalability Considerations
section.t: To reduce the number of packets generated at a regular interval, Backup Advert packets may be sent at a reduced rate as compared to Advert packets sent by the VRRP Active.

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: A VRRP peer that forms a member of this Virtual Router, but does not support this feature or extension must be configured with the lowest priority, and will only operate as the Router of last resort on failure of all other VRRP routers supporting this functionality.

The mechanism defined by this document is intended for deployments where BFD can provide a shorter and operationally reliable failure-detection time than the VRRP Active_Down_Timer, and where the monitored BFD path shares the intended fate with the protected forwarding path. If BFD cannot provide a detection-time advantage, the integration provides no convergence benefit while adding BFD session state, periodic control traffic, configuration, and another operational dependency. In that case, native VRRP failure detection should be used without this integration.

BFD reports reachability of the monitored bidirectional path; it does not by itself determine the health of the remote VRRP process. Therefore, BFD supplements rather than replaces VRRP Advertisements and the Active_Down_Timer. Operators should ensure that filters, policers, shapers, and queueing do not disrupt BFD packet delivery relative to the configured BFD Detection Time.

The operational issues described in Section 8 of continue to apply. The operational considerations described in Section 7 of , including packet treatment, processing load, and the trade-off between protocol overhead and failure-detection time, also apply to this mechanism. Implementations and operators should also follow the generic BFD application guidance in , particularly its description of BFD as an advisory service to client protocols.
This Draft does not preclude the possibility of the peer table being populated by means of manual configuration, instead of using the BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT as defined by the Draft.

section.name: Applicability to VRRPv2
section.t: The workings of this Draft can be extended to VRRPv2 defined in RFC3768, with the introduction of BACKUP ADVERTISEMENT and Peer Table as outlined in the Draft.

front.title: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) Version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6

abstract.t: This memo defines the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) for IPv4 and IPv6. It is version three (3) of the protocol, and it is based on VRRP (version 2) for IPv4 that is defined in RFC 3768 and in "Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol for IPv6". VRRP specifies an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a virtual router to one of the VRRP routers on a LAN. The VRRP router controlling the IPv4 or IPv6 address(es) associated with a virtual router is called the Active, and it forwards packets sent to these IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. VRRP Active Routers are configured with virtual IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, and VRRP Backup Routers infer the address family of the virtual addresses being carried based on the transport protocol. Within a VRRP router, the virtual routers in each of the IPv4 and IPv6 address families are a domain unto themselves and do not overlap. The election process provides dynamic failover in the forwarding responsibility should the Active become unavailable. For IPv4, the advantage gained from using VRRP is a higher-availability default path without requiring configuration of dynamic routing or router discovery protocols on every end-host. For IPv6, the advantage gained from using VRRP for IPv6 is a quicker switchover to Backup Routers than can be obtained with standard IPv6 Neighbor Discovery mechanisms.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs

abstract.t:
Many protocols make use of identifiers consisting of constants and other well-known values. Even after a protocol has been defined and deployment has begun, new values may need to be assigned (e.g., for a new option type in DHCP, or a new encryption or authentication algorithm for IPSec). To insure that such quantities have consistent values and interpretations in different implementations, their assignment must be administered by a central authority. For IETF protocols, that role is provided by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).
In order for the IANA to manage a given name space prudently, it needs guidelines describing the conditions under which new values can be assigned. If the IANA is expected to play a role in the management of a name space, the IANA must be given clear and concise instructions describing that role. This document discusses issues that should be considered in formulating a policy for assigning values to a name space and provides guidelines to document authors on the specific text that must be included in documents that place demands on the IANA.
